summaries.example: You have eaten many red apples, and they were sweet. You expect the next similar apple to be sweet too. That is a reasonable guess from past experience, but it is not guaranteed: the next apple could be sour. The puzzle asks what makes this kind of guess reasonable.
summaries.summary: Induction is the everyday practice of learning from observations. If every similar snack you have tried was safe, you may expect the next one to be safe. David Hume pointed out that past success does not logically guarantee future success. To defend such a prediction, we might say nature usually continues in the same way. But then we need support for that idea. A proof cannot guarantee it, because the future could change without contradiction. An experience-based argument may seem to assume the same pattern it is trying to defend. Hume said that habit or custom explains why people make these predictions, even if habit is not a proof. Later philosophers have offered different responses, including probability, explanations, practical methods, and theories of learning. The entry presents these responses without treating any one answer as settled.
key_ideas: People use past observations to predict future events and make general claims.
David Hume asked what supports these predictions.
A prediction is not certain just because a pattern has continued before.
Hume’s dilemma says that a defense of induction might be too strong to prove or might rely on induction itself.
Some philosophers try probability, explanation, practical success, or learning methods; others accept that the puzzle remains.
summaries.why_it_matters: Induction is behind many ordinary choices and much scientific prediction. It helps us learn from experience, but it also reminds us to separate a strong expectation from certainty. Thinking about induction can make us more careful about evidence, patterns, and predictions.

important_terms.definition: Using things we have observed to make a guess about things we have not observed yet.
The idea that the future will continue to resemble the past in relevant ways.
A careful argument that must be true if its starting points are true.
A habit of expecting similar results after seeing the same pattern many times.

questions_to_think_about: When does a repeated pattern give you a good reason to expect it again?
Can any number of past examples guarantee what will happen next?
Would you trust a prediction more if it had a good explanation?
Is a useful guessing method always a truth-guaranteeing method?

summaries.example: Suppose a medical researcher observes that a treatment helped 95 of 100 patients in a study and predicts that it will help most similar future patients. This is an inductive inference: it moves from observed cases to an unobserved case or broader population. The prediction may be highly probable under a suitable model, but it is not deductively guaranteed. A Bayesian analysis would require assumptions about the model and prior probabilities; an explanation-based approach would ask whether an underlying law or mechanism best explains the observed success.
summaries.summary: The problem of induction concerns the justification of inferences from observed cases to unobserved cases or general laws. Hume analyzes such reasoning through a dilemma. A demonstrative or a priori argument cannot establish the Uniformity Principle—the claim that nature will continue in relevantly similar ways—because its negation is conceivable and therefore not contradictory. An empirical or probable argument appears circular when it supports uniformity by citing the past success of inductive reasoning, since that appeal itself depends on assuming that past success predicts future success. Hume does not deny that people make inductive inferences; he explains their psychological basis through custom and habit. The SEP entry surveys attempts to resist both horns. These include Kantian synthetic a priori reasoning, nomological-explanatory arguments using laws and Inference to the Best Explanation, Bayesian methods, combinatorial proposals, and partial solutions in learning theory. It also examines rule-circularity, views that deny universal inductive rules, entitlement and ordinary-language approaches, pragmatic vindication, formal learning theory, and meta-induction. Some philosophers accept a skeptical conclusion, while others limit or reinterpret its significance for ordinary life and science.
key_ideas: Hume’s dilemma targets the basis of moving from observed regularities to unobserved cases.
The first horn argues that an a priori or demonstrative proof cannot establish that nature will remain uniform, since a change in nature is conceivable.
The second horn argues that an empirical defense of uniformity is circular if it uses the very pattern of successful induction that it seeks to justify.
Hume’s own account explains induction through custom, habit, or imagination rather than a demonstrative chain of reasoning.
Responses include synthetic a priori arguments, law-based explanation, Bayesian probability, combinatorial proposals, and partial learning-theoretic results.
Other approaches change what justification means, defend rule-circularity or practical success, reject universal rules, or accept inductive skepticism.
summaries.why_it_matters: Induction is central to prediction, science, statistics, and machine learning. Hume’s challenge does not show that prediction is useless; it asks what kind of support prediction can have. The debate clarifies the difference between certainty, probability, reliability, practical success, and conformity to accepted standards. It also exposes assumptions that can remain hidden inside models, explanations, and learning procedures.

important_terms.definition: An inference from observed cases to unobserved cases or to a generalization.
The assumption that relevant future regularities resemble relevant past regularities.
Reasoning whose conclusion follows necessarily from its premises; the conclusion cannot be false if the premises are true.
Reasoning that uses empirical information to support a conclusion without making it certain.
The problem that an argument for induction may already presuppose the inductive rule it is meant to establish.
Updating probabilities for hypotheses after receiving evidence.
Inferring that the hypothesis offering the strongest explanation of evidence is probably true.
A weaker defense of a method based on its prospects for achieving practical or epistemic success, rather than proving its conclusions true.

questions_to_think_about: Does showing that a method has worked in the past justify expecting it to work in the future?
Is rule-circularity less problematic than premise-circularity? Why might the distinction matter?
Do Bayesian methods solve the problem, or do their priors and models add empirical assumptions?
Could science rely mainly on testing and rejecting hypotheses rather than extrapolating from past regularities?
What is the difference between a method being rational, useful, and likely to produce true conclusions?

summaries.example: Imagine that your school bus has arrived at 7:30 every school day this month. You predict it will arrive at 7:30 tomorrow. You are using induction: you are extending a pattern from the past to a new case. But the pattern could change because of traffic, weather, or a new schedule. Hume asks why the past pattern should be trusted to continue. Saying “it has always happened before” uses the same kind of reasoning that needs defending.
summaries.summary: Induction is reasoning that moves beyond what has been observed. We use it when we expect tomorrow’s bus to follow its usual schedule or when we generalize from many examples. David Hume’s problem is not whether people make these inferences; they clearly do. His question is what gives them a rational foundation. Hume’s dilemma considers two possible kinds of support. A demonstrative argument would make the conclusion certain, but the future could differ from the past without contradiction. A probable argument uses experience, yet a defense of the Uniformity Principle may rely on the same inductive pattern it is trying to justify. Hume therefore explains our tendency through custom or habit, while philosophers debate whether that is a justification. Proposed responses include Kant’s synthetic a priori approach, arguments from the best explanation, Bayesian probability, and methods from learning theory. Some approaches offer only partial or practical support. Others reject the idea of one rule behind every inductive inference, and some accept skepticism while arguing that everyday reasoning and science can continue.
key_ideas: Induction helps us predict events and form general beliefs from examples.
Hume separates certainty-producing arguments from experience-based arguments.
A deductive proof cannot show that the future must match the past, because a different future is possible without contradiction.
An experience-based defense can be circular if it relies on the past success of induction.
Some philosophers think explanations, probability, or mathematical learning results can provide partial answers.
Other philosophers argue that induction needs no single universal rule, or that the problem changes what we should mean by justification.
summaries.why_it_matters: Induction shapes everyday expectations and scientific theories. Understanding its difficulty helps us notice that repeated evidence can make a belief well supported without making it certain. It also encourages us to ask which assumptions, models, explanations, or goals make a prediction reasonable.

important_terms.definition: Reasoning that uses past observations to predict a new observation or support a general pattern.
The claim that nature will keep behaving in relevantly similar ways over time.
An argument that gives certainty, so that denying its conclusion would create a contradiction.
An argument based on experience that supports what is likely rather than what is certain.
A problem where an argument secretly assumes the point it is supposed to prove.
A method of revising the probability of a hypothesis when new evidence arrives.
Choosing the explanation that best accounts for the evidence.

questions_to_think_about: Why is the bus example reasonable even though it is not certain?
Would a very large number of observations solve Hume’s worry?
Can a good explanation support a prediction without using induction?
What assumptions do probability models require?
Should a method count as justified if it is useful, even when it does not guarantee truth?
